steps.label: Character Sets
steps.content:
Text, Sound and Images

Character Sets

Year 10, 1.2 L1

steps.label: What Is a Character Set?
steps.content:
What Is a Character Set?

A character set assigns a unique binary code to every character a computer needs to store or display.

  • Text is stored as numbers, like everything else in a computer, so every character needs an agreed binary code.
  • A character set is that full list of agreed codes, one per character.
  • ASCII is the most common character set for English text: a 7-bit code (normally stored in 8 bits) giving 128 possible codes.
  • Every device using ASCII agrees on the same 128 codes, so text typed on one computer displays correctly on another.

steps.label: Digits, Space and Case
steps.content:
Digits, Space and Case

  • Digits '0' to '9' are coded 48 to 57 (hex 30 to 39).
  • Space is coded 32 (hex 20).
  • A lowercase letter's code is always its uppercase code plus 32 (one extra bit, the 32-column, switched on).
  • Example: 'H' is 72 (01001000). 'h' is 72 + 32 = 104 (01101000).

This +32 rule works for every letter, not just H, so you can decode or encode a lowercase letter even without it being written out in the table.

steps.label: Why Unicode Is Needed
steps.content:
Why Unicode Is Needed

ASCII works well for English text, but it cannot represent every character the world needs.

  • ASCII has only 128 codes, which is enough for uppercase and lowercase English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters.
  • Other writing systems need thousands more characters: Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Thai, and many more.
  • Unicode is a much larger character set designed to represent the characters used by different languages and many symbols and emoji.
  • Unicode can use different numbers of bytes for different characters, so it is not limited to 128 codes like ASCII.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • Why do two different computers need to agree on the same character set?
  • How many bits does a single ASCII character normally use?
  • What is the binary difference between an uppercase and lowercase version of the same letter?
  • Why can ASCII alone not represent every language in the world?
  • What is stored in a computer's memory when you type the letter 'Z'?

y10_1_2_l1_activity_2.feedback: Look up each byte in the table separately: 01001000, 01000101, 01001100, 01001100, 01001111.
01101000 is 104 in denary, which is lowercase 'h' - notice it is not the same code as capital H.
00110111 is 55 in denary. Digits run 48 to 57, so 55 is the digit '7'.
01101110 is 110 in denary. 'N' is 78, and 110 = 78 + 32, so this is lowercase 'n'.

y10_1_2_l1_activity_3.feedback: B = 01000010, Y = 01011001, E = 01000101. Extra spaces between the bytes are fine.
Take the capital-letter codes from part (a) and add 32 to each: b = 01100010, y = 01111001, e = 01100101.
